text:
Philip Rubin is a distinguished researcher in speech technology and cognitive science, best known for his foundational work on articulatory synthesis, speech perception, and the biological bases of language. During the 1970s at Haskins Laboratories, he developed the ASY (Articulatory Synthesis) and SWS (Sinewave Synthesis) systems, which pioneered the modeling of speech production as a series of dynamic "gestures" rather than static features. Rubin also designed the HADES signal processing system and the SPIEL programming language, a precursor to MATLAB. His theoretical contributions emphasize a dynamical systems perspective, viewing speech as spatiotemporal coordination within embodied systems, and he explored the relationship between acoustic signals and physical vocal tract movements through biomechanical constraints and inverse mapping techniques.
Beyond his academic research, Rubin has held significant leadership roles in science administration, policy, and advocacy. He served as the Director of the Division of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences at the National Science Foundation (NSF) and later as the Assistant Director for Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), where he led the White House's neuroscience initiative. Rubin has also been a prominent figure in science policy, serving as Chair of the National Academies Board on Behavioral, Cognitive, and Sensory Sciences and founding the Auditory-Visual Speech Association. His career spans a wide range of activities, including founding the Yale Macintosh Users Group, serving on the Board of Trustees for the University of Connecticut, and contributing to ethical discussions regarding emerging technologies and human subjects research.
